transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-28 10:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Nova Head of ML), Ethan Green (Nova Infra), Priya Singh (Nova Product), Samir Rao (Nova Security)

Summary: quick check-in on Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policy options, burst behavior seen in last test, and next steps for sustained throughput run. Some audio mis-recognition present; minor acronym slippage (K V cache heard as K V cash).

Topics: sizing recap, observed burst patterns, autoscale cooldowns, reserved capacity vs burst pool, security questions, next steps/tests.

Transcript: 
[00:00:00] Laura: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy holidays early, we'll keep it tight, agenda is sizing and autoscale after the weekend test, Ravi's got the logs.
[00:00:12] Maya: Thanks Laura, yea we saw the spike friday night, was about 2.4x baseline for ~12 minutes, some of that was batched jobs and some real-time user traffic, we wanted to understand if Dedicated can handle that without breaking p95.
[00:00:28] Ravi: Cool, so quick recap — we deployed 6 nodes w/ H100-equivalent, we had autoscale set to +3 nodes max burst and cooldown 5m, the sustained qps baseline is ~120 rps, the peak we saw hit ~290 rps for short bursts.
[00:00:45] Ethan: Quick callout — the client side sends mixed long and short sequences, avg tokens per request around 320 but 10% are 4k tokens, which changes memory/KV cache behavior.
[00:01:03] Diego: Yeah that 4k tail is important, it balloons KV cache and per-token latency, so when we size we need headroom for those heavy requests.
[00:01:18] Maya: Right, so our p95 target is 350ms, p99 under 800ms for interactive flows, batch async can be higher.
[00:01:30] Ravi: With the current setup p95 drifted to ~520ms at peak, but recovered after autoscale added nodes; the problem was cooldown and the initial scheduling, there was a 45s window where new pods were still initializing and requests queued.
[00:01:46] Priya: Is that cold start issue mostly model load time or infra scheduling?
[00:01:52] Ravi: Two parts — model load on GPUs (weights + quant profile) is ~20–30s depending on quantization, scheduling + networking another 15–25s. For H100-like hardware with fast NVMe it was closer to 20s model load.
[00:02:10] Laura: So options we discussed — warm pool (pre-warmed nodes), higher baseline reserved capacity, or faster burst policy with prefetch. Tradeoff is cost vs latency protection.
[00:02:22] Ethan: Can you share the numbers for pre-warm? like how many nodes kept idle to cover a 3x burst?
[00:02:30] Ravi: Rough calc — baseline 6 nodes, for 2.5x you need ~9–10 nodes. If you keep 2 warm nodes we reduce startup latency but you still might see p95 spikes if many 4k requests arrive. Warm pool sizing depends on expected burst concurrency.
[00:02:46] Maya: Our traffic pattern shows 80% of bursts are short-lived (<10m) and 70% of bursts are at night. So warm pool could be small.
[00:02:57] Diego: Also worth noting prefix caching and KV cache can help. If many requests share prefixes, effective cost drops. But you said earlier sequences are diverse?
[00:03:07] Maya: Yeah diversity is high for chat+summaries, but internal batch jobs have repeats.
[00:03:14] Priya: On autoscale policies, can we do a two-tier policy: fast short-term burst with pre-warm + quick ephemeral nodes, and a slower scale for sustained increases?
[00:03:24] Ravi: Absolutely. We typically recommend: 1) pre-warm pool sized to absorb X qps (fast path, instant routing), 2) ephemeral burst nodes with 60–90s aggressive scale-up (handle immediate surge), 3) sustained scaling with longer cooldown (5–10m) to avoid oscillation.
[00:03:41] Ethan: What's the risk of oscillation here? we don't want flapping that keeps adding/removing nodes and kills throughput.
[00:03:47] Diego: That's why cooldown and hysteresis are key. Also batching windows: if you increase batching slightly during bursts you can increase throughput without more nodes, but that affects latency.
[00:03:58] Maya: For customers like us, cost matters; we'd rather accept a 10% p95 hit during rare bursts than double committed capacity.
[00:04:06] Laura: Totally fine — we can model cost curves. We'll provide a few configuration options: low-cost (small warm pool, higher p95 tolerance), mid (moderate warm pool + ephemeral burst nodes), high-availability (reserve capacity to hit SLOs).
[00:04:20] Priya: Can you quantify expected cost delta between low-cost and mid-level?
[00:04:25] Laura: Ballpark—mid is ~1.6x low-cost monthly for the workload you shared, and high-availability ~2.4x low-cost. We'll send a precise estimate in the sizing draft.
[00:04:36] Samir: On security — about KMS and audit logs, the last doc had everything but we need confirmation that key management integrates with our HSM and that audit logs show per-request model version.
[00:04:48] Ravi: We support customer-managed KMS (Cloud KMS or HSM), and can surface per-request model id in audit logs. We'll include the SOC2 docs and the trace examples.
[00:04:58] Maya: Great, please add sample log snippet.
[00:05:02] Diego: Back to sizing — we ran the 2-hour load test last week; attached spreadsheet shows qps vs p95. Quick note: transcription earlier mis-labeled some things, the file mentions K V cash instead of KV cache, sorry for that.
[00:05:16] Laura: No worries. Ethan, any infra constraints on number of GPUs per VPC?
[00:05:22] Ethan: We have a soft limit of 32 GPUs in our current VPC, bump-request in progress, but for Dedicated we'd likely use a private CIDR with dedicated hosts, so that may not be a blocker long-term.
[00:05:35] Maya: For the sustained 6-hour test you suggested, what's the ideal pattern? constant qps at 150, or replay sampled traffic?
[00:05:44] Ravi: Prefer replay of real traffic with some amplification to cover tail cases — maintain baseline for 4 hours and inject scaled bursts (2x–3x) for 30–60 minute windows. We'll provide a test plan template.
[00:05:58] Priya: How do we measure cost during tests? we'd like per-token cost and per-request CPU/GPU utilization metrics.
[00:06:05] Diego: We'll share telemetry: per-token compute time, GPU utilization, and Redwood Console export with token-level breakdown. That will feed into the cost model.
[00:06:15] Laura: Ok quick recap of sizing decisions so far — recommended mid-tier: baseline 8 nodes, pre-warm pool 2 nodes, ephemeral burst up to +4 nodes, autoscale aggressive scale-up for <90s and cooldown 5m for ephemeral, sustained scale cooldown 10m. This should hold p95 ~350–420ms for most bursts and keep cost reasonable.
[00:06:37] Maya: Sounds good; small question — are those node counts guesstimates for H100-class or A100?
[00:06:43] Ravi: H100-class baseline. If you want A100 we'll adjust numbers (A100 needs ~1.2–1.4x nodes depending on quant profiles).
[00:06:52] Ethan: For burst >2x we saw queuing at the ingress LB. Any suggestions?
[00:06:58] Diego: Increase concurrency at the front-end, use per-route routing with overflow policy to fallback small model variant for non-critical requests, and tune ingress LB buffer sizes.
[00:07:12] Priya: We might accept degraded model for non-critical flows during bursts — what about automated fallback?
[00:07:18] Ravi: Redwood supports automatic fallback rules to smaller variants or lower-precision quantized models; we can set route-level policies so critical routes never fallback.
[00:07:28] Maya: Ok, that's useful.
[00:07:31] Laura: Action items — Ravi will draft dedicated sizing doc, Diego test plan, Ethan provide traffic histogram, Laura send pricing + SOC2. Any other asks?
[00:07:40] Samir: Please include retention options for logs — 90 days vs 1 year and cost delta.
[00:07:46] Laura: noted.
[00:07:50] Priya: About billing — can you show a blended rate for pre-paid reserved vs usage for bursts?
[00:07:57] Laura: Yes we will break out reserved monthly + burst billing in the estimate.
[00:08:02] Maya: One last question — during the 45s init window you mentioned, were requests dropped or queued?
[00:08:08] Ravi: They were queued at ingress and some timed out at client at the tail; client timeouts caused retries which exacerbated the spike. We'll model client-side retry backoff as part of runbook.
[00:08:18] Ethan: Could we add a soft-fail policy to return priority-based errors to avoid retries?
[00:08:24] Diego: Yes, a 429 with Retry-After and informing clients is recommended; plus a small circuit breaker on client.
[00:08:32] Maya: Ok that helps.
[00:08:36] Laura: Great — let's confirm owners and dates. Ravi (sizing doc) by Jan 4, Diego (test plan) by Dec 31, Ethan to share histograms by Dec 30, Laura to send pricing + SOC2 by Dec 29.
[00:08:48] Maya: Thanks, we'll review and come back with any gaps. Happy holidays all.
[00:08:53] Laura: Thanks everyone — closing.

Notes and references: attached spreadsheet mentioned in call (link: https://redwood.app/sheets/poc-nova-traffic), SOC2 doc (link: https://redwood.app/security/soc2-sample), sizing template (link: https://redwood.app/templates/dedicated-sizing).
